items.explanation: The drawing is part of a patent application: legal paperwork through which Bell claimed the telephone as his invention. That is what the document directly shows — an inventor securing legal rights. It does not show government funding, and the drawing depicts the device, not a national network, which Bell did not personally construct. Patents were meant to encourage commercialization by protecting inventors, not to block it. The document illustrates the first step of the era's pattern: inventors claimed ideas legally, while organizing capital and building businesses — the step that produced the great fortunes — was largely separate work.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — Bell's telephone (1876) + PD patent drawing, 1876 (stimulus)

option_explanations.A: Nothing in a patent application shows government funding; patents are private legal claims, not grants of public money.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The document is Bell legally claiming his invention — the inventor's step. Building the telephone business was done by organizers and investors, a separate step.
option_explanations.C: The drawing shows the telephone device, not a network, and Bell did not personally construct a nationwide system.
option_explanations.D: Patents did the opposite: by protecting an inventor's claim, they encouraged investors to commercialize new ideas.

options: (A) The federal government funded most of the era's important inventions through direct grants and supervised their commercial development.
(B) Inventors used the patent system to claim legal ownership of their ideas, which entrepreneurs and investors then built into businesses.
(C) Bell personally designed, financed, and constructed the nationwide telephone network depicted in the drawing.
(D) Patent law blocked new inventions from reaching the market by denying inventors any legal protection for their work.

items.explanation: Edison's 1879 bulb made electric light practical, and its economic importance was extending usable hours: factories, stores, and streets could be lit brightly and safely after dark. Gas lamps were replaced gradually over decades, not in a year. Early electric lighting served cities, not isolated farmhouses. Bulbs consumed electricity generated largely by coal-burning stations; they did not end coal demand.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — Edison's light bulb (1879) 'rewired daily life'

option_explanations.A: Adoption took decades; no technology replaced a whole lighting system in one year.
option_explanations.B: Early electric service was an urban phenomenon — power stations served dense city districts.
option_explanations.C: Light bulbs use electricity; the power stations that supplied it burned coal.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Practical electric light extended the business day and rewired daily life.

options: (A) replaced every gas lamp in American cities within a single year of its invention, ending the gas-lighting era almost overnight
(B) was adopted mainly in isolated rural farmhouses, where gas lines could not reach and no other lighting alternative existed
(C) ended the demand for coal entirely, since the new bulbs generated their own electric power without burning any fuel
(D) made electric lighting practical for factories, shops, and streets, extending the hours when business could be done

items.explanation: Menlo Park was a private research laboratory: a team of workers developing inventions as organized, paid work. That was the significant change — invention becoming a business function. It was not a university or a government project. Independent inventors kept working long after 1880; Menlo Park added a new model rather than ending the old one.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — Edison's light bulb (1879) + PD photograph of Menlo Park laboratory, late 1870s (stimulus); organized-R&D interpretation flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: This was a private business laboratory, not a university.
option_explanations.B: No government agency directed or funded this work.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The photograph shows invention organized as team-based, business-funded work.
option_explanations.D: Overstatement: independent inventors continued working for decades afterward.

options: (A) proved that American universities had taken over scientific research from private businesses by the late 1870s
(B) showed that the federal government directed and funded the era's most important technological research programs
(C) turned invention into organized, team-based work funded by business rather than the effort of a lone inventor
(D) meant that independent inventors stopped inventing entirely after 1880, leaving all research to corporations

items.explanation: The engraving literally shows the infrastructure work: crews burying electric lines for a new power station. Electricity could not piggyback on gas pipes; it needed its own system. The work shown is happening in New York City in 1882 — urban first, not small towns first — and it was underway, not delayed for decades.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — Edison's light bulb (1879) 'rewired daily life' + PD Harper's Weekly engraving, June 21, 1882 (stimulus)

option_explanations.A: Correct. The image shows the new infrastructure — buried lines for a new power station — being built.
option_explanations.B: The scene is New York City; electrification began in dense urban districts.
option_explanations.C: The workers are laying new electric lines, not reusing gas pipes.
option_explanations.D: The 1882 date shows the work happening, not delayed.

options: (A) It required building an entirely new infrastructure — wires, stations, and equipment — beneath and above city streets.
(B) It was adopted first in small towns, where installation was cheapest and where existing systems were simplest to convert.
(C) It needed no new construction because the electric lines could simply be run through the existing gas pipes.
(D) It was delayed for decades because city governments refused to allow any of the necessary construction work.

items.explanation: Pearl Street was the first central power station: it generated electricity in one place and sold it to customers nearby. That business model — power as a utility service — was as important as the machinery. The dynamo certainly had business significance. Edison's company charged customers; it did not give power away. The station served part of lower Manhattan, not the whole country.
items.fact_source: PD photograph (Edison's Jumbo dynamo, Pearl Street — described as Edison's first electrical power plant) + u6.md §The story — Edison's light bulb (1879); utility-business interpretation flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: The dynamo's whole purpose was commercial: generating power to sell.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Central generation plus paying customers made electricity a utility business.
option_explanations.C: Edison's station was a commercial venture; customers paid for the power.
option_explanations.D: Overstatement: the station served nearby customers in lower Manhattan.

options: (A) a technical one only: the dynamo itself, an impressive machine whose importance was purely mechanical rather than commercial
(B) producing electricity in one central station and selling it to many nearby customers, making power a business
(C) giving electricity away free to the public in order to prove to everyone that electric light was better than gas
(D) powering the entire United States from a single large building located in lower Manhattan

items.explanation: Owning every stage from raw materials to finished product is vertical integration — owning every step from mine to market, as Carnegie did in steel. Horizontal integration means buying out competitors at the same stage, as Rockefeller did with refineries. A trust combines separate companies under one board to limit competition. Collective bargaining is negotiation between a union and an employer.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Vertical / horizontal integration — Controlling every production stage (Carnegie)... owning every step from mine to market

option_explanations.A: Correct. Controlling each production stage — mines, fuel, transport, mills — is vertical integration.
option_explanations.B: Horizontal integration is buying out rival firms at the same stage, not controlling successive stages.
option_explanations.C: A trust combines competing companies under one board; it does not mean owning the supply chain.
option_explanations.D: Collective bargaining is union-employer negotiation, not a business-ownership strategy.

options: (A) vertical integration
(B) horizontal integration
(C) a trust
(D) collective bargaining

items.explanation: Before Bessemer, steel was too expensive for large-scale use; the process made it cheap, which is why rails, bridges, and skyscrapers became economical. Iron had been made for thousands of years — Bessemer made steel affordable. Steel mills still employed thousands of workers. Wood remained a common building material.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Bessemer process — Cheap steelmaking method adopted in the 1870s; made skyscrapers, rails, and bridges economical

option_explanations.A: Iron predates the Bessemer process by millennia; the breakthrough was cheap steel.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Cheap steel is what made rails, bridges, and skyscrapers economical.
option_explanations.D: Overstatement: wood stayed cheap and widely used in construction.

options: (A) was the first method ever devised for making iron in any form throughout history
(B) allowed factories to operate entirely without employing any workers at all
(C) made steel cheap enough to use for rails, bridges, and tall buildings
(D) ended the use of wood in all American construction projects permanently

items.explanation: The Bessemer process of the 1870s lowered steel's cost, which made a steel bridge across the Mississippi affordable; building such projects then expanded the market for steel producers — a feedback loop between technology and business. The causation in the first option is reversed: the process came first. The bridge carried rail and road traffic, not primarily telegraph wires. The Eads Bridge was a private enterprise, not proof that private firms couldn't build big things.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Bessemer process (1870s; made bridges economical) + §The story — Bessemer process made steel cheap in the 1870s

option_explanations.A: Reversed causation: the Bessemer process (1870s) made the steel bridge possible, not the other way around.
option_explanations.B: The bridge carried railroads and roadways; telegraph wires were incidental.
option_explanations.C: The bridge was privately built — evidence that private firms could finance giant projects.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Cheap steel enabled the bridge, and the bridge (and others like it) fed demand back to steelmakers.

options: (A) Bridge building created the commercial demand that directly caused the invention of the Bessemer process.
(B) Steel bridges were built mainly to carry telegraph wires across wide rivers.
(C) The bridge proved that private companies could no longer afford large-scale construction projects on their own.
(D) Cheaper steel made giant projects possible, and those projects then created still more demand for steel.
items.stem: The Eads Bridge across the Mississippi at St. Louis, completed in 1874, was one of the first major bridges built with steel. Its construction best illustrates which relationship between technology and business?

stimulus.image_caption: The Eads Bridge across the Mississippi River at St. Louis, completed 1874 — among the first major bridges built with steel.

items.explanation: A steel bridge on this scale required cheap steel, which only existed after the Bessemer process was adopted in the 1870s. The steel industry remained private — no nationalization occurred. Engineers had built many bridges before; the barrier was the cost of steel, not know-how. Wood stayed cheap and widely used.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Bessemer process — adopted in the 1870s; made... bridges economical

option_explanations.A: The steel industry stayed in private hands throughout the Gilded Age.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Only cheap Bessemer steel made a steel bridge of this size affordable.
option_explanations.C: Engineers had built many bridges; the new factor was affordable steel.
option_explanations.D: Wood remained cheap and common as a building material.

options: (A) the federal government had nationalized the steel industry in the 1870s
(B) the Bessemer process had made steel affordable in the 1870s
(C) American engineers had never built a bridge of any kind before
(D) wood had become too expensive for any construction work

items.explanation: The image is a criticism of concentrated corporate power: Vanderbilt bestrides the country like a giant, suggesting the railroads had grown beyond democratic restraint. It is caricature, not a literal claim that one man laid all the track. The tentacles show reach and strength, not weakness. No railroad breakup had occurred in 1879.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — Railroad barons... built empires + PD cartoon (Judge, 1879, Keppler; verified subject: William Henry Vanderbilt)

option_explanations.A: Correct. The giant figure expresses the cartoonist's criticism: railroad corporations had become dangerously powerful.
option_explanations.B: Caricature is not literal reporting; the point is power, not track-laying.
option_explanations.C: The spreading tentacles show overwhelming reach — the opposite of weakness.
option_explanations.D: No such breakup occurred in 1879; the railroads were at the height of their power.

options: (A) railroad corporations had grown powerful enough to dominate the economy and threaten democratic control
(B) Vanderbilt personally laid every mile of railroad track in the entire country with his own hands, working unaided
(C) railroads were too weak and disorganized to connect the nation's far-flung markets
(D) the government had already broken up all the railroad companies into small local lines
